entities.name: Umayyad Caliphate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Umayyad Caliphate (661–750 CE) was the second Islamic caliphate, founded by Muawiyah I after the First Islamic Civil War. The largest empire in history up to that point, the Umayyads expanded from Spain and Morocco in the west to the borders of China and India in the east, spreading Islam across three continents in less than a century.

Muawiyah I's establishment of the Umayyad caliphate in Damascus transformed Islam from a prophetic movement to an imperial administration. Arabic became the language of administration across the empire. The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem (691 CE) and the Great Mosque of Damascus (706-715 CE) were built under Umayyad patronage, establishing Islamic monumental architecture. The conquest of the Iberian Peninsula (711-719 CE) introduced Islamic civilization to Europe.

The Umayyad expansion brought Islam's greatest military achievements but also its most controversial political developments: the marginalization of non-Arab Muslims (mawali) and the transformation of the caliphate into an Arab monarchy generated resentment that fueled the Abbasid Revolution of 750. A surviving Umayyad prince, Abd al-Rahman I, escaped to Spain and established the Emirate of Córdoba, preserving the dynasty until 1031 CE. Córdoba under Umayyad rule became medieval Europe's largest and most sophisticated city.
